role: Incense Maker at a Family Incense Workshop
headline: A daughter who studied Chinese materia medica in Fuzhou and came home to her family's three-generation incense workshop in Dapu, Yongchun: an incense maker who, from first light, mixes the paste, rolls the sticks, dries them in the sun and dyes their bamboo feet red, learning to take over her father's craft between temple orders for the Ghost Festival and agarwood orders from Malaysia
unit: A three-generation family incense workshop in Dapu township, Yongchun, Quanzhou (shop in front, workshop behind, a dozen or so veteran workers)
education: Bachelor's degree in Chinese materia medica
level: You can take a batch through mixing, rolling, sun-drying and dyeing the feet on your own, and you know the properties of the herbs better from the books than your father does. But your sticks still come out uneven, your judgment of when the clouds mean bringing the incense in is always half a beat slow, and your father won't yet let you near blending a formula.
intro: Your family in Dapu has made incense for three generations; your grandfather's generation carried it on shoulder poles to the Chinese communities of Southeast Asia. You went to Fuzhou to study Chinese materia medica. Your classmates went into pharmaceutical plants and hospitals; you came home after graduating. As of today you work beside your father, starting from a bundle of bamboo splints and a basin of incense paste, taking the craft into your own hands bit by bit.
salary_note: Estimate: a family incense workshop in Yongchun earns by the order. The run-up to the Ghost Festival and to Spring Festival is high season; the rest of the year is slow. Family members take a share of profits rather than a wage, which works out to thirty or forty percent below the national average a month, and in a good year can double.

facts.label: Incense Maker (current level)
facts.value: 1-3 years, ¥3,000–4,700 a month (at this employer, estimated)

facts.label: What AI can't take
facts.value: Opening a batch from cellar aging and inspecting it

facts.label: Where AI is moving in
facts.value: Grinding a batch of incense powder to a formula, mixing the paste and forming it

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 0 related listings nationwide, 0 in this city (mostly campus hiring and internships)

day: It's barely light and your father is already in the courtyard reading the sky: no clouds in the east, wind coming down off the hills, a drying day. You pull on your old sleeve covers and pin up your hair.

In the back workshop you mix the paste: sandalwood powder, agarwood dust, a few powdered herbs, nanmu wood powder as the binder, water added a little at a time. Your father pinches the paste you've mixed and says one shade softer, or it'll shed when you roll it.

You sit on a low stool rolling incense, a handful of bamboo splints turning in your palm: wet, roll in powder, wet again, roll again. The old woman beside you, forty years at this, rolls a bundle twice as fast as you, every stick the same thickness as if from a mold.

You fan the bundles out on bamboo racks and wheel them onto the drying ground. Every household on the street is drying too, red feet facing outward, and from the top of the slope it looks like a field in bloom.
Half-dried incense gets its feet dyed. You dip the bamboo ends of each bundle into red dye, lift and shake them. At noon you wash your hands, and the red under your nails won't come out.

Dark clouds rise beyond the hills and your father shouts: bring it in. The whole family and the workers haul the racks indoors, and the last few bundles are barely through the door when the rain crashes down.

In the shop, the steward of a temple in Quanzhou has come to order incense for the Ghost Festival rites, two thousand bundles, and bargains hard. You do the sums beside him while your phone lights up with a message from an old customer in Malaysia asking for samples of agarwood coils.

At night in the main hall you light one of today's sticks to test it, watching whether the smoke rises straight, what color the ash is, whether it smells different at the start and at the end, and note it all down in your book.

ladder.title: Incense Apprentice / Incense Assistant
ladder.focus: Learn the materials, grind powder and mix paste, do basic forming and help with hands-on classes. You move up as your hands steady. Pay when starting out is generally low.

ladder.title: Incense Maker
ladder.focus: Carry out preparation of materials, forming and cellar aging on your own, keep output consistent and lead hands-on classes.

ladder.title: Incense Artisan
ladder.focus: Blend formulas and develop new products on your own, take on custom orders, and teach and spread incense culture.

ladder.title: Studio Owner / Head of Product Development at an Incense Company
ladder.focus: Run a brand shop or studio, or lead a product line at an incense company.

ladder.title: Intangible Heritage Bearer / Master Incense Artisan
ladder.focus: Pass on the craft, train apprentices, and take part in occupational standards and industry events.

ai_tasks.name: Opening a batch from cellar aging and inspecting it
ai_tasks.how: AI can help record and compare the tasting notes from each opening. Smelling it, watching how it burns and deciding whether it ships or ages longer takes a person's nose and experience, and a person answering for it.

ai_tasks.name: Grinding a batch of incense powder to a formula, mixing the paste and forming it
ai_tasks.how: AI or software can convert recipes, keep batch records and remind you of the production schedule. Weighing the materials, grinding and sifting, the feel of how soft the paste is, rolling balls, pressing molds and cutting sticks are handwork done by a person.

ai_tasks.name: Preparing a batch of incense herbs
ai_tasks.how: At most, AI can help look up what the classical texts say about preparation. Deciding how to clean a herb and draw out its fragrance from the state it's in depends on a person's senses and hands.

ai_tasks.name: Leading a hands-on class in incense seal powder or incense tablets
ai_tasks.how: AI can help prepare the script, slides and little stories about incense culture. Showing students how to make seal incense and tablets on the spot, correcting their technique and looking after how each person is doing is done by a person.

ai_tasks.name: Creating a custom room fragrance for a client and revising the formula again and again
ai_tasks.how: AI can organize the client's wishes, turn vague descriptions into scent keywords, draft formula directions and log every revision. Testing again and again, adjusting proportions and talking through the trade-offs with the client is something a person has to oversee.

ai_tasks.name: Reconstructing an ancient formula and turning it into a teaching case
ai_tasks.how: AI can search the old texts, set out the differences between versions and draft a course outline. Actually reconstructing it, testing whether the combination and preparation hold up, and judging whether the conclusions can be taught is done by a person.

events.e_storm: An afternoon thunderstorm comes in too fast, with more than thirty racks still out on the drying ground. The soaked paste breaks out in blotches. Your father takes one look and says knock it all off and start again. The whole day's work is gone.
events.e_nanyang: An old customer at a clan association in Singapore sends word for a whole shipping container of incense, saying his grandfather's generation burned your family's. On packing day you tuck a handwritten card into every carton.
events.e_machine_next: The incense factory next door installs an automatic rolling machine. One machine does the work of ten old women a day, and their factory price is thirty percent below yours. When the temple steward comes to haggle, the first thing he mentions is them.
events.e_ban: City after city promotes civilized worship, and scenic spots and temples begin limiting incense: three sticks a person, no giant sticks. Your orders for big bundles shrink every year, while orders for fine sticks and aromatherapy grow.
events.e_fake: You buy a lot of agarwood from a dealer in Guangdong, and while grinding it something smells wrong. You test-burn it and the finish is pure synthetic fragrance. You send the whole lot back, and from then on you light a piece of every material yourself before buying.
events.e_agarwood: The price of agarwood doubles in a year, and the cost of several of your old formulas doubles with it. You and your father talk it over all night and decide not to change the materials: raise the price, make less.
events.e_study_tour: A busload of primary school children on a study trip comes from Quanzhou, and you teach them to roll incense, one stick each to take home. A little girl holds up her crooked one and asks: teacher, will it break halfway when it burns?
events.e_expo: You take your family's incense to an intangible heritage fair in Fuzhou. Most of the people who stop at your stand are young. They don't ask what it's for; they ask what it smells like. You say: like the hills after rain.
events.e_ai_texts: You use AI to compare different editions of several old incense manuals, which formula has an extra ingredient, which describes a preparation differently, all listed in minutes. But which version actually works, you still find out pot by pot.
events.e_ai_words: Setting up the online shop, AI helps you turn a customer's "like my grandmother's wardrobe" into a string of scent keywords and drafts several formula directions. One version says to add camphor. One sniff and you know it's wrong.
events.e_archive: You start keeping a file on every batch: where the materials came from, which day it was dried, the weather and humidity, what you smelled at the start, middle and end of the test burn. Going through the files three years later, for the first time you can explain why paste mixed in the plum-rain season always needs half a day more in the sun.
events.e_dust: The days of grinding are dusty, and even with a mask you cough for a week. Your father says he was the same when he was young, and that was when he put an extraction fan in the grinding room.
events.e_cold: You catch a cold, and for a whole week your nose smells nothing. All the test burns those days go to your father, and you sit beside him watching him smell with his eyes closed, as if he were listening to something.
events.e_typhoon: A typhoon passes through, knocking down half the racks on the drying ground and lifting tiles off the back workshop's roof. The next day the whole family is up on the roof fixing tiles, while the old women below spread the wet incense powder out bag by bag to dry.
events.e_father_ill: Your father's back gives out and he's laid up for two months. That Ghost Festival's orders all fall on you. For the first time you read the sky and bring in the incense alone, and bargain alone with the temple stewards, and at night when you lie down your hands are still shaking.
events.e_notebook: Your father hands you the formula book your grandfather left. The paper has gone brittle, and many characters are written in folk spellings of the Minnan dialect. You photograph it page by page, circle the ones you can't read, and on weekends take them to an old scholar in town.
events.e_wedding: You get married, to a teacher at the township middle school. The workshop stops for the day of the wedding, and your father lights a stick of an old formula he blended himself. The whole house fills with that scent.
events.e_child: Your child is born. At the one-month celebration you carry the baby around the drying ground, and each of the old women touches the tiny hand and says: an incense roller's hand, someday.
events.e_old_worker: The old woman who rolled incense for forty years says her eyes have gone and she won't be coming anymore. Before she leaves she gives you the rolling board she used half her life, a shallow groove worn into the middle of the wood.
events.e_viral: A video you shot of incense drying spreads online: a whole slope of red feet, with the sound of wind off the hills. That month the online orders jump tenfold, and you and the workers put in overtime for a month.
events.e_young_leave: Of the two young apprentices you hire, one quits after three months because of the sun, and the other after six for a bubble tea shop in Xiamen. You don't try to keep them. You save the bundles they ruined to show the children on study trips.
events.e_hands: After more than twenty years of rolling, the knuckles of your right hand ache whenever it rains. You hand the rolling to your apprentices and keep only the mixing, the blending and the test burns for yourself.

c_machine.title: Whether to buy a rolling machine
c_machine.situation: The temples bargain harder every year, and your father is torn over buying an automatic rolling machine: it would halve the labor cost and speed up delivery. But then the old women would have no work, and your incense wouldn't be much different from next door's.

options.label: Buy it; bulk orders go to the machine
options.result: The machine rolls the big bundles for the festival rites, and the old women roll only the fine sticks and agarwood for longtime customers. That year, for the first time, you deliver without fighting the deadline. Your father says you should have bought it long ago, then adds: who knows if it's right.

options.label: Stay with handwork
options.result: You lose two temples' big orders and keep a few old customers who will only buy hand-rolled. An old gentleman in Singapore writes to say he can smell the difference.

c_cert.title: Sit the vocational skill grading for Incense Artisan
c_cert.situation: Incense artisan has been added to the national list of occupations, with official skill-level certification. Your father says a craft doesn't depend on a piece of paper, but when Quanzhou's culture and tourism bureau, schools and study-trip operators invite someone to teach, the first thing they look at is that certificate. It means two weeks of training in Quanzhou, right in the best drying weather.

options.label: Sit it
options.result: The practical exam has you blend a formula on the spot and explain the roles of sovereign, minister, assistant and envoy. When you get to the preparation of one herb, the examiner asks where you learned it. From the books, you say, and from my father. When the certificate arrives your father says nothing, and hangs it on the shop wall.

options.label: Not yet; the drying comes first
options.result: Your incense dries better those two weeks than ever, not one batch redone. Later the study-trip company invites a certified master from the next township to teach, and you see it on social media.

c_online.title: Open an online shop and make incense for young people
c_online.situation: You want to open an online shop selling small boxes of fine incense sticks, room fragrance and incense tablets to young people who don't worship. Your father says those are trinkets, not incense. But temple orders are falling, and it would mean filming videos, answering messages and redoing packaging every night, without letting any of the day's work slide.

options.label: Open it
options.result: You name your first incense Hills After Rain and make a little handwritten box for it. In the first three months you sell fewer than a hundred boxes; in the fourth, someone writes a long review online, and orders suddenly pick up.

options.label: Stick with the old customers
options.result: You put all your effort into the temples and the old overseas customers and make every batch faultless. But each year's orders are a little thinner than the last.

c_xiamen.title: Open an incense space in Xiamen
c_xiamen.situation: A college friend runs a tea space in Xiamen's old town and wants you as a partner in an incense space: sales in front, classes in back, lots of tourists, each customer spending several times what they would in your township. But the workshop can't be left untended and your father is getting on; you could only come back two days a week.

options.label: Go to Xiamen
options.result: Every Wednesday night you take the bullet train back to Yongchun, and every Friday morning back to Xiamen. The classes at the incense space are fully booked, and what tourists ask most is: did you roll this yourself? You say my family did.

options.label: Stay in Dapu
options.result: You don't go. Your friend's incense space later stocks someone else's incense. You visit once, smell it, say nothing, drink a pot of tea and leave.

c_perfume.title: A Shanghai fragrance company asks you to be a perfumer
c_perfume.situation: A fragrance company in Shanghai has seen your incense online and wants you as a perfumer, making room scents, perfumes and collaborations. Three times what you make at home, a laboratory, thousands of raw materials. But that's perfumery with fragrance oils, a different thing from mixing paste and rolling sticks, and you'd be leaving the workshop.

options.label: Go to Shanghai and make perfume
options.result: You wrap the grooved rolling board in a cloth and put it in your suitcase.
options.end: You work many years as a perfumer in Shanghai, making lobby scents for hotels and entrance scents for malls. Every year around the Ghost Festival you take a few days off and go back to Yongchun, and sit at the edge of the drying ground watching the slope of red incense feet, for a whole afternoon.

options.label: Stay at the workshop
options.result: You turn them down. That afternoon in the back workshop you blend a new formula using an old herb from your grandfather's book, and when you test-burn it, your father stands behind you smelling it for a long time.

c_archive.title: Whether to keep a file on every batch
c_archive.situation: You want to turn the formulas, material sources and sensory notes for every batch into a searchable archive, with AI helping to organize and compare it, so whoever takes over can look it up. Your father says incense lives in the nose and the hands; what good is it in a computer? It would cost you an extra hour or two every night.

options.label: Build it
options.result: You record batch after batch: what you smell at the start, middle and end, whether the ash is white or gray, whether the smoke rises straight. Two years later an overseas customer says this year's incense is different from ten years ago, and you pull up the files and compare them for him line by line.

options.label: Never mind; trust the nose
options.result: Like your father, you keep what matters in a notebook and in your nose. The notebook grows thicker and thicker, and only you can read it.

c_studio.title: Take over the workshop as its owner
c_studio.situation: Your father says he can't keep it up and wants to hand the workshop to you as owner: managing the workers, the materials, the books and the brand, and keeping up with the temples and the old overseas customers. A big incense company in Quanzhou has also come to you, offering the job of head of product development: one product line, no worrying about wages or weather.

options.label: Take over the workshop
options.result: You repaint the shop sign, leaving the characters unchanged. In the first year you lose two and a half kilos, and for the first time the ledger shows income from the online shop and study trips, more than from the temples.

options.label: Go to the big company for R&D
options.result: In the company lab you bring out four new products in a year, with test reports and standards. On weekends you go home, and your father is still alone in the back workshop mixing paste. You roll up your sleeves and help.

c_heritage.title: Apply to be an intangible heritage bearer
c_heritage.situation: The county is nominating a group of bearers of Yongchun incense as intangible cultural heritage, and your family's branch can put forward only one. You've worked at it for over a decade, and the formulas and archives are in your hands. But your cousin has made incense half his life and is ten years older, and the clan elders all feel he should go first.

options.label: Apply yourself
options.result: Your application includes three generations of formulas, more than ten years of archives and photos from hundreds of study-trip classes. On the day the list is published your cousin says nothing, and at New Year he still comes over for tea.

options.label: Let your cousin go first
options.result: You give your cousin the material you compiled, and he is accepted. The elders say you know how things are done, and whenever your cousin gives a talk afterward, he mentions that you put it all together.

c_school.title: A vocational school asks you to teach incense
c_school.situation: A vocational school in Quanzhou has opened a program in incense culture and incense products and invites you to be a full-time teacher: leading students in preparing herbs, blending and designing study-trip courses, with a permanent state post and winter and summer breaks. But the workshop would pass to the workers and apprentices, and your family's three-generation craft would live on in a school.

options.label: Go and teach
options.result: You photocopy your grandfather's formula book and lock the original in a cupboard at home.
options.end: You teach incense in Quanzhou for many years, and your students scatter to incense workshops, incense companies and cultural venues across Fujian. Every graduation season a few of them mail you the first formula they've blended themselves. You light a stick and smell it with your eyes closed for a long time.

options.label: Stay with the workshop
options.result: You say the workshop can't do without you. The school has you give two talks a term, and you go with a bundle of bamboo splints and a basin of paste, and the students end up with powder all over their hands.

endings.retire: On the last good drying day, you don't go out onto the drying ground. You sit in the bamboo chair by the door watching your apprentices fan the bundles out. The wind comes down the slope, and the red feet all along the street sway gently. You light a stick of your grandfather's old formula, set it in the censer by the door, and watch its smoke rise straight up.
endings.burnout: That year your hands and your cough flare up together, and the doctor tells you to stay away from incense powder. You hand the workshop to your apprentices and move into the county town, walking in the park every morning. When you catch a scent of incense drifting from someone's house, you still stop to tell whether it was rolled by machine or by hand.

stages: You can carry a batch through preparation, mixing, rolling, sun-drying, dyeing and cellaring on your own, and answer for its quality. Every day you roll incense with the old women in the back workshop, learn from your father to read the clouds and bring the racks in, and at night test-burn in the main hall and keep your notebook. When children come on study trips, you can lead a hands-on class. On blending formulas, your father hasn't given way yet.

You start blending formulas yourself: reconstructing the old ones from your grandfather's book first, then changing them herb by herb into your own, with burn and scent tests. You take custom orders from temples, exclusive blends for overseas clan associations and room scents for young people, working out with customers in the shop, line by line, the scent they're after. Culture venues and schools invite you to talk about incense, and what you talk about is your own drying ground.

What you run now is the whole workshop: scheduling a dozen workers, deciding where materials come from, keeping the books, building the brand. By day you deal with material dealers, temple stewards, online shop customer service and study-trip companies; at night you go through the archives and blend new formulas. The rolling has passed to your apprentices; the final test burn, and the decision whether a batch ships, are yours.

More of your time goes into passing it on: training apprentices, organizing three generations of formulas and preparation methods, sitting on occupational standards and heritage review panels, and talking about Yongchun incense at schools, fairs and clan associations overseas. The workshop's daily running is in your apprentices' hands, but every day you still walk through the back workshop, pinch the paste to feel how soft it is, and glance at the sky over the drying ground.
work: The old woman says today's paste is too sticky; it clings to the hands when rolling. You work in another handful of nanmu powder and a little sandalwood, knead it ten minutes and roll again, and the sticks come out smooth.

An old man buying for a temple picks up a bundle, looks at the red of the feet and says the color is paler than last year's. You dig out the dye invoices and switch suppliers, and at the second batch he nods.

You open a batch of coil incense that has been cellared six months and light a coil. The start is a little sharp; the finish is lovely. You write: another three months. Then you tie the crate up again with hemp rope.

The owner of a tea space in Xiamen wants an incense to go with oolong that won't fight the tea. You make five versions, and in the last you drop the clove and add a touch of roasted aged tangerine peel. She sips her tea, sniffs, and says: this one.

Reconstructing an old formula from your grandfather's book, you find one herb is meant to be honey-roasted. You try the heat three times; on the third, roasted just until faintly golden, the sweetness finally comes out in the incense.

A teacher leading a study trip asks what incense really has to do with Chinese medicine. You take out angelica root and lovage rhizome, break off a little of each for the children to smell, then light a stick containing both and let them smell the smoke.

You negotiate next year's agarwood price with the old dealer from Guangdong, and he quotes thirty percent more. You don't haggle; you only ask that he send you a small piece of every lot to test-burn first, and that a failed lot goes back whole. He thinks it over and signs.

A batch of fine sticks from an apprentice keeps snapping halfway through burning. You check the archive and find humidity was high those days, so you have him use a tenth less water in the paste and dry it half a day longer. The second batch never snaps.

A museum comes to discuss a collaboration: an incense recreating the scene in an ancient painting. You spend an afternoon in the back workshop with their curator, and the formula you settle on has only five ingredients.

At a skill-grading review, one candidate's incense contains synthetic fragrance. You don't say so on the spot. After the grading you talk with him alone for half an hour and show him how natural materials can reach that scent too.

A clan association in Malaysia invites you to speak about Yongchun incense. You bring a bundle of splints and a basin of paste and roll incense in the association's courtyard for the old people, and one old man says he saw it done in your township when he was little.

You turn three generations of formulas and twenty years of batch files into a set of course notes. The last page isn't a formula but something your father said: watch the sky, watch your hands, watch the smoke.
past: You go to middle school in Dapu, and the first thing you do after school is help bring the incense in from the drying ground. Your classmates think you always smell of incense. You can't smell it yourself.

Your gaokao (college entrance exam) gets you into a university of Chinese medicine in Fuzhou to study Chinese materia medica. Your father says that's good: when you blend incense, you'll know the nature of every herb.

In your second year you study herb preparation, and when the teacher covers honey-roasting, wine-processing and vinegar-processing, you think of the big iron wok in the back workshop at home, and after class you go ask whether incense herbs are prepared the same way.

At graduation your classmates go to pharmaceutical plants, hospitals and drug testing institutes, and you get an offer from a pharmaceutical company. Your father calls. He doesn't ask you to come back; he only says there are too many Ghost Festival orders this year to keep up. You go home.

In your first year back you learn from the old women, starting with rolling, and ruin hundreds of bundles over one summer. In the month before the Ghost Festival you check a whole batch's quality alone for the first time, and your father corrects only one thing.

late.pension_note: Estimate: a family workshop has no employer paying social insurance, so you pay into the pension yourself as a flexibly employed person, on a low base. The basic pension comes to a little over thirty percent of your usual monthly income, and you live mainly on the workshop's profit share and savings.
scenes: In your first month no longer running the workshop, you still wake a little after five and open the window to look at the eastern sky. Only after looking do you remember that whether to dry today is no longer yours to decide.
Before every batch ships, your apprentices still bring you a stick to test-burn. After smelling it you say just one word: fine. Or: wait.
You plant angelica, mint and a few pots of jasmine in the courtyard, and on summer evenings you sit by them, telling which scent the wind brings first.
Your grandchild comes back from the city and you teach him to roll a stick, crooked as anything. You light it by the door and it snaps halfway, and you both laugh.
After moving into the county town you don't touch incense powder for a long time, and the red on your hands fades away. For the first time, the skin under your nails is white.
Once the cough clears, you do tai chi in the park every morning with the others, then sit in the pavilion smelling the incense drifting from a distant temple and guessing whose family made it.
Your apprentice has grown the workshop and invites you back to cut the ribbon. You stand at the door a moment, reach out and pinch a lump of freshly mixed paste, and say: a shade too soft.
In your first year away from the workshop, whenever clouds rise over the hills in the afternoon your heart still skips, and you almost shout to bring the incense in.

You go back to Dapu for the Ghost Festival. The whole street is still drying incense, only now more of it is machine-rolled than hand-rolled. On your family's drying ground, an apprentice is fanning out the red feet bundle by bundle.
A student you taught has opened a workshop in Quanzhou and mails you a box of incense, handwritten on the lid: Hills After Rain, second version.

The township builds an incense culture museum, and on its wall hangs an old photo from many years ago: a little girl on a drying ground holding a bundle of incense, standing beside her grandfather. The guide says nobody knows who she is. You don't say.
You find your grandfather's formula book in the cupboard, the paper even more brittle. You don't open it again. You only smell it through its cloth wrapping, and the scent is still there.

closing.retire: Many years later, one evening, you sit in the bamboo chair by the door. The incense on the drying ground has been brought in, and the air still holds a little sandalwood and sunshine. Clouds are rising on the distant hills. You watch them a while and know it won't rain tonight.
closing.burnout: Many years later, on a balcony in the county town, you light a stick of a formula you blended many years ago and watch the smoke climb slowly to the eaves and spread. You watch until it burns out. The ash is white, and it never broke.
closing.end: Many years later, at the bottom of a trunk, you find the grooved rolling board, the wood still warm to the touch. You rub your palm back and forth in the groove twice, as if you were still holding a bundle of bamboo splints, then put it back where it was.
